note: Breakfasts, packable lunches, and the component recipes — sauces, roasts, snacks — that the dinners lean on. Component recipes are tagged 'component' and are what turn leftovers into a second meal.

recipes.title: Heart-Smart Overnight Oats
recipes.blurb: Five minutes on Sunday night, four breakfasts done. Oat beta-glucan plus chia plus walnuts is about as heart-forward as a bowl gets.
steps: Stir oats, chia, soy milk, yogurt, maple, cinnamon and vanilla together in a bowl until there are no dry pockets.
Divide into four jars. Press the berries down into the mix rather than sitting them on top so they bleed color and flavor overnight.
Refrigerate at least 6 hours, up to 5 days.
Add walnuts in the morning, not the night before — they go soft otherwise. Add banana slices to order.
variations: Peanut butter and banana: 2 tbsp peanut butter stirred in, banana on top.
Apple pie: grated apple, extra cinnamon, chopped pecans.
Chocolate: 2 tbsp cocoa and an extra tablespoon of maple. This is the version that wins children over.
recipes.kidTweak: Let each kid pick their own jar's toppings on Sunday. Ownership does more for breakfast compliance than any amount of persuading.
recipes.restaurantTouch: A pinch of flaky salt on top of the chocolate version. It sounds wrong and it is not.
recipes.garden: Summer berries straight into the jar.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 5 days. Make a double batch Sunday and Wednesday.
recipes.heartNote: About 3 g of oat beta-glucan a day is the amount tied to measurable LDL reduction. One of these jars gets you most of the way there.

recipes.title: The Green One
recipes.blurb: Three minutes, one blender, and it is genuinely green rather than green-adjacent. Flax and soy milk for the heart, frozen banana for the texture.
steps: Liquid first, then soft, then frozen — that order is why some blenders jam and others don't.
Blend the soy milk, yogurt, spinach and flax first until completely smooth and no flecks remain. This is the step that makes it drinkable for a suspicious eight-year-old.
Add the frozen banana, berries, almond butter and cinnamon. Blend 45 seconds until thick.
Pour and drink within a few minutes — it separates.
recipes.kidTweak: Blend the spinach into the liquid completely before adding berries. Once the berries go in it turns purple and nobody asks questions.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Freeze the bananas in chunks. Fresh banana makes a thin smoothie; frozen makes it milkshake-thick with nothing added.
recipes.garden: Spring spinach straight from the bed.
recipes.leftovers: Pour extras into popsicle molds. That is dessert solved too.

recipes.title: Soft Scrambled Eggs with Wilted Greens
recipes.blurb: Low and slow, off the heat before you think, with greens wilted into the pan first. Ten minutes and it eats like a hotel breakfast.
steps: Beat the eggs and whites with salt until the color is completely uniform — streaky eggs cook unevenly.
Wilt the spinach with the garlic in the oil over medium, 2 minutes, until the water has cooked off. Scrape it onto the toast.
Wipe the pan, set it over low heat — genuinely low — and add the eggs. Stir constantly with a rubber spatula, pushing curds from the edge to the center.
After 3-4 minutes they will start to set into small soft curds. Pull the pan off the heat while they still look slightly underdone; carryover finishes them.
Fold in parmesan and scallions. Pile onto the greens and toast with black pepper and avocado.
recipes.kidTweak: Cook a kid's portion a minute longer and skip the greens under theirs — put the spinach on the side where they can ignore it, which is how they eventually try it.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Low heat and constant motion. That is the entire difference between diner eggs and restaurant eggs.
recipes.garden: Spring spinach and chives.
recipes.leftovers: None. Scrambled eggs do not keep and everybody knows it.
recipes.heartNote: Six whole eggs across four people is a moderate serving. The extra whites add protein without cholesterol.

recipes.title: Blueberry Baked Oatmeal
recipes.blurb: Bake it Sunday, cut it into squares, and breakfast is handled through Thursday. Reheats in ninety seconds and tastes like a muffin.
steps: Heat oven to 375°F and oil a 9x13 dish.
Whisk soy milk, eggs, maple, mashed banana and vanilla. Stir in oats, flax, baking powder and cinnamon.
Fold in most of the blueberries, pour into the dish, and scatter the rest of the berries and the walnuts over the top.
Bake 35-40 minutes until set in the center and golden at the edges.
Cool 10 minutes before cutting into 8 squares.
recipes.kidTweak: Serve warm with a splash of cold milk poured over. Chocolate chips instead of half the blueberries buys a lot of goodwill.
recipes.restaurantTouch: A spoon of Greek yogurt and a drizzle of maple on the plate turns a square of baked oatmeal into a café breakfast.
recipes.garden: Summer berries, obviously — and rhubarb in May if you have a patch.
recipes.leftovers: 5 days refrigerated, 3 months frozen in individual squares. Microwave 90 seconds from frozen.

recipes.title: Everything Avocado Toast with Smashed White Beans
recipes.blurb: The beans are what make it hold you until lunch — 15 grams of protein instead of 4, and it takes an extra ninety seconds.
steps: Toast the bread hard — properly crisp, so it does not collapse — and rub each slice with the cut side of a garlic clove while it is still hot.
Smash the beans with the olive oil, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt until rough and spreadable.
Smash the avocado separately with the rest of the lemon juice. Keeping them separate gives you two textures instead of one gray paste.
Spread beans first, avocado on top, then everything seasoning, pepper flakes and tomatoes.
recipes.kidTweak: Kids generally want avocado alone on toast, cut into strips. Fine — put the beans on the side with a spoon.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The hot-toast garlic rub. It is a thirty-second habit from Spanish kitchens and it changes toast permanently.
recipes.garden: Cherry tomatoes and a few basil leaves in August.
recipes.leftovers: None — make it to order.

recipes.title: Vanilla Chia Pudding
recipes.blurb: Four ingredients, ten seconds of stirring, and 10 grams of fiber per cup. The kids treat it as dessert; that is fine.
steps: Whisk chia, soy milk, maple and vanilla. Wait 5 minutes and whisk again — that second whisk is what prevents a clump at the bottom of the jar.
Refrigerate at least 3 hours or overnight.
Top with strawberries and toasted almonds. For the chocolate version, whisk the cocoa in at the start.
recipes.kidTweak: Chocolate version, layered with yogurt in a clear glass, reads as a parfait and disappears.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Layer it: pudding, fruit, pudding, fruit. Same food, completely different reception.
recipes.garden: June strawberries.
recipes.leftovers: 5 days.

recipes.title: Smashed Chickpea Salad Sandwiches
recipes.blurb: Tastes like the tuna salad you grew up on, built on chickpeas and Greek yogurt instead of mayo. Fifteen minutes and it packs for lunch all week.
steps: Smash the chickpeas with a masher or fork until about two thirds are broken down and a third stay whole. Texture is everything here.
Fold in yogurt, Dijon, celery, red onion, dill, lemon juice, capers, salt and pepper.
Taste and adjust — it usually wants more lemon and more pepper than you expect.
Build the sandwiches with lettuce against the bread on both sides so it does not go soggy in a lunchbox.

omnivore.label: Add canned tuna
omnivore.note: Half the chickpea mix plus a drained can of tuna is a natural for the omnivores.
steps: Fold the drained tuna into half the mixture.

recipes.kidTweak: Serve it as a scoop with crackers and cut vegetables instead of a sandwich. Same food, more likely eaten.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Rinsed chopped capers. A tablespoon adds the briny pop that makes people ask what is in it.
recipes.garden: Dill, and lettuce in spring and fall.
recipes.leftovers: The salad keeps 4 days. Do not build the sandwich until you are eating it.

recipes.title: Greek Chickpea Jar Salads
recipes.blurb: Four lunches built in ten minutes on Sunday. Dressing on the bottom, greens on top, and nothing is soggy on Thursday.
steps: Whisk olive oil, lemon juice, vinegar, oregano and Dijon. Divide among four jars — dressing always goes in first.
Layer in this order and do not improvise it: chickpeas and red onion (they marinate), then cucumber and tomatoes, then quinoa, then feta and olives, then romaine packed on top.
Seal and refrigerate up to 4 days. Shake into a bowl when you eat.
recipes.kidTweak: Build a kid's version in a divided container instead: chickpeas, cucumbers, cheese, crackers. A jar you shake is an adult format.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Marinating the onion and chickpeas in the dressing for days is not a compromise — it is genuinely better than dressing a salad at the last second.
recipes.garden: Cucumbers and tomatoes at their July peak.
recipes.leftovers: That is the entire point. 4 days.

recipes.title: Thermos Tomato-Lentil Soup
recipes.blurb: Thirty minutes, blends smooth, and holds heat in a thermos until noon. The lunch that gets a kid through a February school day.
steps: Cook onion and carrot in oil 8 minutes. Add garlic and spices 45 seconds, then tomato paste for a minute.
Add lentils, crushed tomatoes, broth and salt. Simmer 22 minutes until the lentils have dissolved.
Blend smooth with an immersion blender. Finish with lemon juice.
Pour boiling water into the thermos and let it sit while the soup finishes — a preheated thermos keeps soup hot until noon; a cold one does not.
recipes.kidTweak: Smooth is the whole strategy. Send crackers or a buttered roll alongside.
recipes.restaurantTouch: A swirl of yogurt and a drizzle of olive oil on top when it is served at home.
recipes.garden: Nothing needed — this is the deep-winter recipe.
recipes.leftovers: 5 days refrigerated, 3 months frozen in single-serving jars.

recipes.title: Black Bean and Spinach Quesadillas
recipes.blurb: Twelve minutes, four ingredients you already have, and a vegetable the kids will not fight about because they cannot see it.
steps: Wilt the spinach in a dry skillet, 90 seconds, then chop it fine and squeeze out the water in a towel. Wet spinach makes a soggy quesadilla.
Mash the beans roughly with the cumin and smoked paprika.
Spread beans over half of each tortilla, then spinach, cheese and scallions. Fold.
Cook in a dry or barely oiled skillet over medium, 3 minutes a side, pressing with a spatula, until the outside is spotted brown and the cheese has melted.
Rest 60 seconds before cutting — cutting immediately is how the filling escapes. Serve with salsa and yogurt.
recipes.kidTweak: Let them dip. A small dish of salsa and a small dish of yogurt turns lunch into a project.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Cook them dry, not in butter. A dry pan crisps the tortilla into layers; fat makes it greasy and soft.
recipes.garden: Spinach in spring and fall.
recipes.leftovers: Reheat in a skillet, never a microwave.

recipes.title: Build-a-Bowl (the Formula)
recipes.blurb: Not a recipe so much as an equation: grain plus roasted vegetable plus protein plus sauce plus crunch plus acid. Learn it once and you never need a recipe for lunch again.

ingredients.prep: dry — or quinoa, or brown rice

steps: GRAIN: cook 1 cup dry farro like pasta in salted water, 25 minutes, drain. Makes about 3 cups.
ROASTED: toss vegetables and dried chickpeas with 2 tbsp oil and salt; roast at 425°F for 25-30 minutes.
SAUCE: whisk tahini, lemon, garlic, a pinch of salt and cold water until pourable.
PICKLE: cover the sliced onion with red wine vinegar and a pinch of salt while everything roasts. Twenty minutes is enough.
CRUNCH: toasted pepitas, or toasted panko, or the crispy chickpeas.
ASSEMBLE in that order — grain, roasted things, sauce, pickle, crunch, herbs — and finish with black pepper and the last of the olive oil.
The rule: every bowl needs something soft, something crisp, something acidic, and something fatty. If a bowl tastes boring, it is missing acid.

omnivore.label: Add any leftover protein
omnivore.note: Sliced chicken, salmon, a jammy egg — the formula does not care.
steps: Warm and slice; lay on top.

recipes.kidTweak: Same components, arranged in separate piles rather than layered, with sauce in a small cup.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The quick pickle. Every good grain bowl in every good restaurant has one, and it takes twenty minutes of doing nothing.
recipes.garden: Whatever is ripe goes in the roasted slot.
recipes.leftovers: Components keep 4-5 days separately. This is how Sunday cooking becomes four lunches.

recipes.title: Whipped Lemon Hummus
recipes.blurb: Ice water and a long blend are what make hummus fluffy instead of pasty. Five minutes, and it beats anything in a tub.
steps: Blend the tahini, lemon juice and garlic alone first, for a full minute, until it is pale and thick. Doing this before the chickpeas go in is the single biggest difference between good and mediocre hummus.
Add chickpeas, cumin and salt; blend 2 minutes, scraping down.
With the motor running, add 3-4 tbsp of ice water a spoonful at a time until it turns fluffy and almost mousse-like.
Spread in a shallow bowl with the back of a spoon, pour olive oil into the well, dust with smoked paprika.
recipes.kidTweak: Serve with carrot sticks, cucumber coins and pita triangles. Hummus is one of the most reliably eaten vegetables-adjacent foods there is.
recipes.restaurantTouch: The swoosh. Spread it wide and shallow with a spoon and pool the oil in the middle — never serve hummus in a mound.
recipes.garden: Nothing, unless you count garlic — and you should grow garlic.
recipes.leftovers: 5 days. Press plastic against the surface so it does not skin over.

recipes.title: House Lemon-Dijon Vinaigrette
recipes.blurb: One jar, ninety seconds, and you never buy bottled dressing again. A quarter of the sodium and none of the additives.
steps: Put everything in a jar, seal it, and shake hard for 30 seconds. The Dijon is the emulsifier — without it the dressing separates in a minute.
Taste on a leaf of lettuce, not off a spoon. Dressing always tastes too sharp alone.
Keeps two weeks refrigerated. It solidifies cold — that is the olive oil, and it is a sign of good oil. Let it sit out 10 minutes and shake again.
recipes.kidTweak: An extra teaspoon of maple syrup or honey makes it a dressing kids will actually put on salad.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Three parts oil to one part acid is the classic ratio; this runs closer to 2:1 because bright dressing makes vegetables taste better and lets you use less salt everywhere else.
recipes.garden: A tablespoon of chopped herbs — chives, dill, basil — turns it into a different dressing every week.
recipes.leftovers: 2 weeks refrigerated.
recipes.heartNote: Bottled ranch runs about 260 mg sodium per 2 tbsp. This runs about 50.

recipes.title: Everything Tahini Sauce
recipes.blurb: The sauce that makes roasted vegetables into dinner. Four ingredients, two minutes, keeps a week.
steps: Whisk tahini, lemon juice, garlic and salt. It will seize into a stiff paste and look ruined. It is not.
Whisk in cold water a tablespoon at a time — usually 4 to 6 total — and it will suddenly turn pale, smooth and pourable.
Thin further for drizzling, leave thicker for dipping.
recipes.kidTweak: Add the teaspoon of maple. It takes the edge off the sesame bitterness that kids notice and adults don't.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Grate the garlic on a microplane rather than mincing it so there are no raw chunks.
recipes.garden: Herbs blended in make a green tahini that is even better.
recipes.leftovers: 1 week refrigerated. It thickens; whisk in water.

recipes.title: Any-Vegetable Roast (the Method)
recipes.blurb: One temperature, one technique, every vegetable. This is the skill that makes vegetables the best thing on the plate instead of the obligation.

ingredients.prep: florets — or substitute any vegetable below

steps: 425°F, always. Lower and vegetables steam; higher and the outside burns before the inside softens.
Cut everything the same size, then toss with enough oil that every surface is glossy — under-oiling is the most common reason home roasted vegetables are leathery instead of caramelized.
Spread on the pan with actual space between pieces. Two pans is not a failure, it is the recipe. Crowding is the second most common reason.
Put the cut sides down and do not stir for the first 15 minutes. Contact with hot metal is where browning happens.
TIMING: broccoli, cauliflower, asparagus, green beans 20-25 min. Brussels sprouts, carrots, sweet potato, squash 25-35 min. Zucchini, peppers, onions 20 min. Tomatoes 25 min.
Finish with acid off the heat — lemon, a splash of vinegar, or balsamic. That final squeeze is what makes people go back for more.
recipes.kidTweak: Roast a batch of 'broccoli trees' or 'carrot coins' with nothing but oil and salt. Kids often reject seasoning, not vegetables.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Preheat the sheet pan in the oven and add the vegetables to hot metal. Immediate sizzle, better crust.
recipes.garden: This is the method that absorbs anything the garden produces in quantity.
recipes.leftovers: 4 days. Cold roasted vegetables belong in tomorrow's grain bowl, eggs, or a sandwich.

recipes.title: Garlicky Greens in Ten Minutes
recipes.blurb: Kale, chard, spinach — the technique is identical and it takes one pan and ten minutes. This is the side dish that goes with everything in this app.
steps: Start the garlic in cold oil over medium and let it come up to temperature slowly, 2-3 minutes, until it is barely golden. Garlic dropped into hot oil burns before it flavors anything.
Add pepper flakes, then the greens with the water still clinging from washing. Toss with tongs.
Cover and cook 3 minutes, then uncover and cook 2-3 more until any liquid has evaporated.
Off heat: salt and lemon juice. Toasted almonds if you want crunch.
recipes.kidTweak: Kids and kale are a long negotiation. Chopped small and folded into pasta with a lot of parmesan is where most families start.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Slice the garlic instead of mincing it. Sliced garlic goes sweet and nutty; minced garlic burns.
recipes.garden: Lacinato kale is a nine-month crop in this climate, and chard regrows all summer from the same plants.
recipes.leftovers: 3 days. Fold into eggs, soup, or pasta.

recipes.title: Crispy Roasted Chickpeas
recipes.blurb: The snack that replaces the chip bag. Six grams of fiber a serving and they cost about fifty cents.
steps: Heat oven to 400°F. Dry the chickpeas on a towel and roll them around — genuinely dry, or they steam. Rub off any loose skins.
Toss with oil only (no spices yet) and roast 35-40 minutes, shaking twice, until they rattle and one crushes with a crack.
Toss with the spices and salt while hot. Spices added before roasting scorch and turn bitter.
Cool uncovered. They crisp further as they cool.
recipes.kidTweak: Cinnamon and a teaspoon of maple instead of the savory spices makes a sweet version that goes in a lunchbox.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Scatter them over salads, soups and grain bowls in place of croutons.
recipes.garden: None.
recipes.leftovers: Best the same day. Store uncovered at room temperature — a sealed container makes them chewy overnight.

recipes.title: Almond-Date Energy Bites
recipes.blurb: No bake, no added sugar, five minutes in a food processor. The after-school food that is not a granola bar wrapper.
steps: Pulse the almonds and oats until coarsely ground, about 15 pulses.
Add dates, cocoa, chia, vanilla and salt. Run the processor 45-60 seconds until the mixture climbs the sides and holds together when you squeeze it.
If it is crumbly, add a teaspoon of water at a time. If it is sticky, another spoon of oats.
Roll into 20 balls. This is the part to hand to the kids.
Refrigerate 30 minutes to firm up.
recipes.kidTweak: This is the recipe children should make. Rolling is the entire job and they eat what they make.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Roll half of them in cocoa powder or toasted coconut so the plate has two things on it.
recipes.garden: None.
recipes.leftovers: 2 weeks refrigerated, 3 months frozen. Eat them straight from the freezer.
recipes.allergenNote: Contains tree nuts. Sunflower seeds substitute one-for-one.

recipes.title: The Everyday Big Salad
recipes.blurb: Enough of a salad to be dinner. The rule is five textures, and once you see it you cannot unsee it.
steps: Dry the greens properly. Wet greens repel dressing and it pools at the bottom of the bowl — a salad spinner is the highest-value ten dollars in a kitchen.
Whisk oil, lemon, Dijon and pepper in the bottom of the big bowl, then pile the sturdy things on top: carrots, cucumbers, chickpeas, cranberries.
Add greens last and toss with your hands from the bottom up, twenty seconds, until every leaf is barely coated.
Top with avocado, pepitas and feta. Five textures: crisp, creamy, chewy, crunchy, juicy. Check that you have all five.

omnivore.label: Add any leftover protein
omnivore.note: Sliced chicken, flaked salmon, or a jammy egg.
steps: Slice and fan over the top of individual plates.

recipes.kidTweak: Give a kid a plate of the components in rows instead of a tossed bowl. Salad refusal is usually about mixing, not vegetables.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Dress in the bowl you built it in and toss with your hands. Never pour dressing over the top of a finished salad.
recipes.garden: June through October this salad is 80% backyard.
recipes.leftovers: Dressed salad does not keep. Store components separately.

recipes.title: Miso Butter Mushrooms on Toast
recipes.blurb: Mushrooms cooked past the point where they give up their water and start to brown, in butter cut with white miso. On thick toast this is lunch; on a small plate it is the thing people ask you to make again.
steps: Heat the olive oil in a skillet over high until it shimmers. Add the mushrooms and do not salt them yet — salt draws out water and water is the enemy of browning.

Cook 6-8 minutes, stirring rarely. They will release liquid, the pan will look wrong, and then the liquid will cook off and they will start to sizzle and brown. Wait for that second stage. Most mushroom disappointment is a pan turned off during stage one.
Lower to medium. Add the butter, garlic and thyme, and cook 2 minutes.
Stir the miso and soy sauce together with a tablespoon of water and pour it in. It will coat everything and reduce to a glaze in about a minute.
Off the heat, add the lemon juice and pepper. Toast the bread properly — dark, so it stays crisp under the mushrooms — and pile them on. Parsley and parmesan on top.
recipes.kidTweak: Miso is savory in a way some kids read as strange. Cook their share of the mushrooms in butter and a pinch of salt only, and put them on buttered toast cut into strips.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Rub the hot toast with a cut clove of raw garlic before the mushrooms go on. It takes four seconds and it is the difference between mushrooms on bread and a dish.
recipes.garden: Thyme and parsley grow in a windowbox. Mushrooms are the one thing here you buy — though a shiitake log in a shady corner is a genuinely rewarding project.
recipes.leftovers: The mushrooms keep 3 days and are excellent stirred into eggs or pasta. Toast fresh bread every time.
recipes.heartNote: Miso is a fermented salt paste — a tablespoon is around 630 mg of sodium on its own, which is most of the 903 mg here. Halve the miso and add a squeeze more lemon and it lands near 600 mg with almost no loss of savor.

recipes.title: Crispy Smashed Potatoes with Garlic Aioli
recipes.blurb: Boiled until soft, squashed flat, then roasted hard so every ragged edge turns to glass. There is no better potato, and the five-minute lemon-garlic aioli is why the pan comes back empty.
steps: Boil the potatoes in heavily salted water 18-22 minutes, until a knife goes through with no resistance at all. Undercooked potatoes will not smash; they will crumble.
Drain and let them steam dry on the pan for 5 minutes. Surface moisture is what stops them crisping.

Heat the oven to 450°F. Spread the potatoes on an oiled sheet pan and press each one flat with the bottom of a glass or a measuring cup — about half an inch thick, with ragged edges. The edges are the best part, so do not aim for neat discs.
Drizzle over the olive oil, making sure it gets into the cracks, and season with pepper and rosemary.
Roast 30-35 minutes without turning, until the undersides are deeply browned and the edges have gone glassy. Resist flipping — one committed side beats two half-hearted ones.
Whisk the mayo, yogurt, grated garlic, lemon juice and mustard. Let it sit at least 5 minutes so the raw garlic mellows.
Serve hot, with the aioli on the side and chives over the top.
recipes.kidTweak: These are the crispest thing on the table and usually need no help at all. Give them plain aioli without the garlic if raw garlic is too sharp — mayo, yogurt, lemon and mustard alone is still very good.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Salt them one final time the second they come out of the oven, while the surface is still hot enough to take it. Salt on a cooled potato just sits there.
recipes.garden: Potatoes are one of the most satisfying things to grow in Northeast Ohio — plant seed potatoes around St. Patrick's Day and dig small waxy ones in July, which is exactly the size this wants.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 3 days. Re-crisp in a 425°F oven for 8 minutes; the microwave turns them to steam.
recipes.prepAhead: Boil and smash them a day ahead and keep them on the pan in the fridge. Roasting is then hands-off.

recipes.title: Lemon Dutch Baby
recipes.blurb: Batter poured into a screaming hot buttered skillet, and twenty minutes later a pancake the size of the pan climbs up the sides and comes out looking like something that should not be possible at home.
steps: Put the skillet in the oven and heat both to 425°F. The pan has to be genuinely hot before the batter touches it — that initial blast of steam is the entire lift mechanism.

Blend the eggs, warm milk, flour, sugar, vanilla, salt and lemon zest for 30 seconds until completely smooth and a little frothy. Cold eggs and cold milk give you a flat one; room temperature matters here more than it usually does.
Let the batter rest 10 minutes while the oven comes up.
Pull the hot pan out, drop in the butter and swirl until it is foaming and coats the sides, then pour the batter straight into the middle. Return it to the oven immediately.
Bake 18-22 minutes. Do not open the oven before 18 — it will deflate and it will not come back. It is ready when the sides have climbed the pan and gone deep brown and the center is set.

It will sink within a minute of coming out. That is what it does, and it is meant to. Hit it with lemon juice and powdered sugar and scatter the blueberries over the crater. Serve straight from the pan with yogurt.
recipes.kidTweak: Watching it rise through the oven door is most of the appeal for a kid — turn the light on and let them. Serve with maple instead of lemon if they prefer.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Dust the powdered sugar through a small sieve from a foot above the pan. Fine and even, not clumped, and it lands like snow.
recipes.garden: Blueberries need acidic soil, which Northeast Ohio does not naturally have — but they do well in a large container with peat-based mix, and two bushes will feed a family's breakfasts through July.
recipes.leftovers: Eat it within ten minutes. A Dutch baby is a moment rather than a dish, and reheating it produces a rubbery pancake.
recipes.heartNote: Four eggs across four servings is 214 mg of cholesterol each, which is the whole reason for the score. Dietary cholesterol turns out to have far less effect on blood cholesterol than saturated fat does for most people, which is why the 2015 US guidelines dropped the 300 mg-a-day cap. If a clinician has told you to watch eggs specifically, this is one to share four ways rather than two.

recipes.title: Austin Breakfast Tacos
recipes.blurb: Soft eggs, crisp potato, salsa and a warm tortilla. Texas eats these every morning and they take fifteen minutes.
steps: Fry the diced potato in the oil over medium-high with the paprika and half the salt, undisturbed for the first 5 minutes, then turning, 12 minutes total until crisp.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt. Cook them in the butter over low heat, stirring constantly with a spatula, 4-5 minutes. Low and slow gives you soft curds; high heat gives you rubber.
Pull the eggs off the heat while they still look slightly underdone — they keep cooking in the pan.
Warm the tortillas directly over a flame or in a dry skillet until they puff and blister.
Build: cheese first so it melts against the hot tortilla, then eggs, potato, beans, salsa, avocado, cilantro.

omnivore.label: Bacon or chorizo
omnivore.note: Cook it first and fry the potatoes in the fat. That is the Austin taqueria way.

recipes.kidTweak: Cheese and egg only, folded into a small tortilla. Salsa on the side.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Cheese against the tortilla, not on top. It melts into a layer that holds the taco together.
recipes.leftovers: The potato and beans keep 4 days; scramble eggs to order.

recipes.title: Chilaquiles Verdes
recipes.blurb: Tortilla chips simmered in salsa verde for exactly one minute, so they soften without collapsing. Mexico's greatest breakfast and a use for stale tortillas.

ingredients.prep: cut into wedges and baked crisp

steps: Bake the tortilla wedges at 400°F for 12 minutes with a little oil until crisp, or use a bag of thick restaurant-style chips.
Broil the tomatillos, jalapeños, onion and garlic until blackened in spots, 8 minutes. Blend with the cilantro, broth and salt.
Fry the salsa in the oil in a wide skillet for 5 minutes until it darkens and thickens — Mexican sauces are always fried, and this is where the flavor concentrates.
Fry the eggs in a second pan, sunny side up.
Add the chips to the simmering salsa and fold for no more than a minute. They should be coated and just yielding, with some crunch left. Longer and you have soup.
Serve immediately with an egg on each portion, queso fresco, crema, red onion and avocado.

omnivore.label: Shredded chicken
omnivore.note: Stir poached shredded chicken into the salsa before the chips go in.

recipes.kidTweak: Serve the chips and salsa side by side rather than combined, with the egg on top.
recipes.restaurantTouch: One minute in the sauce. Chilaquiles are eaten immediately — this is a dish with a two-minute window and everyone in Mexico knows it.
recipes.leftovers: The salsa keeps 10 days and freezes. Assemble to order.

recipes.title: Menemen
recipes.blurb: Turkish soft-scrambled eggs cooked into peppers and tomato until it is almost a stew. Fifteen minutes, one pan, eaten with bread and no cutlery.
steps: Cook the peppers in the olive oil over medium heat for 8 minutes until completely soft. Turkish cooks use long green sivri peppers; a green bell is the closest common substitute.
Add the tomatoes, pepper flakes and salt and cook 6-8 minutes until the mixture thickens and the oil separates out at the edges.
Turn the heat to low, pour in the eggs, and stir slowly with a wooden spoon. Menemen is meant to stay soft and loose — take it off the heat while it still looks a little wet.
Crumble the feta over, scatter parsley, and bring the pan to the table with a lot of bread. There are no plates in this recipe.
recipes.kidTweak: Leave the pepper flakes out. Eggs and tomato with bread for scooping is an easy morning.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Grate the tomatoes on a box grater and discard the skin. Thirty seconds, and no skin curls in the pan.
recipes.leftovers: Eat immediately; scrambled eggs do not keep.

recipes.title: Savory Miso Oatmeal
recipes.blurb: Oats cooked in broth instead of milk, with miso, a jammy egg and scallions. Once you have had savory oats the sweet version starts to seem strange.
steps: Soft-boil the eggs: 7 minutes from boiling, then ice water. Peel and halve.
Brown the mushrooms in the sesame oil for 5 minutes.
Add the oats and broth and simmer 5 minutes, stirring, until thick and creamy.
Stir the spinach in to wilt. Take the pan off the heat before whisking in the miso — boiling miso loses its aroma completely.
Top each bowl with an egg, scallions, sesame seeds and chili crisp.
recipes.kidTweak: Not the recipe for a cautious eater. Make theirs with milk, cinnamon and fruit from the same pot of oats before the broth goes in.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Miso off the heat, always. It takes two seconds to get right and it is the difference between savory and flat.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 2 days and thickens solid; loosen with broth.
recipes.heartNote: Oat beta-glucan with about 8 g of protein and no added sugar. A serving of savory oats runs roughly a third the sugar of a flavored instant packet.

recipes.title: Buckwheat Buttermilk Pancakes
recipes.blurb: Nutty, tender and a genuine whole grain. The batter rests ten minutes while the pan heats, which is what makes them rise properly.
steps: Whisk the dry ingredients. Whisk the buttermilk, eggs and melted butter separately.
Combine with a few strokes and stop while it is still lumpy. Overmixed pancake batter makes tough pancakes, every single time.
Rest the batter 10 minutes while the griddle heats over medium. The flour hydrates and the baking powder gets a head start.
Cook 2-3 minutes until bubbles form and the edges look dry, then flip once and cook 90 seconds more. One flip only.
Serve with maple syrup and blueberries. Keep them warm in a 200°F oven in a single layer, never stacked — stacked pancakes steam and go limp.
recipes.kidTweak: Let them drop the blueberries onto each pancake after it hits the griddle. Distribution improves and so does buy-in.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Melted butter in the batter, not just on the griddle. It is why diner pancakes taste better than yours.
recipes.leftovers: Freeze flat in a bag with parchment between. They toast straight from frozen.

recipes.title: Freezer Breakfast Burritos
recipes.blurb: One hour on Sunday, twelve breakfasts in the freezer. Ninety seconds in the microwave and they are genuinely good, not just convenient.
steps: Roast the sweet potato, pepper and onion with the oil, chili powder, cumin and half the salt at 425°F for 25 minutes.
Scramble the eggs softly with the remaining salt — stop them while they are still glossy, because they cook again on reheating and dry eggs are what ruin freezer burritos.
Wilt the spinach in the residual heat of the egg pan and squeeze out any water.
Let everything cool to room temperature before assembling. Warm filling steams inside the wrap and gives you a soggy burrito and freezer ice.
Build each burrito with cheese first, then eggs, vegetables, beans and a spoonful of salsa. Fold the sides in, then roll tightly.
Wrap each in parchment, then freeze on a tray before bagging. To reheat: unwrap, microwave 90 seconds, flip, 45 seconds more — or 20 minutes at 350°F wrapped in foil.
recipes.kidTweak: Make a few without the chili powder. Label them.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Cheese against the tortilla on both sides of the filling. It seals the wrap and stops moisture getting into the bread.
recipes.leftovers: Three months in the freezer. Do not refrigerate more than 3 days unfrozen.
recipes.heartNote: About 21 g protein and 9 g fiber each, and roughly a third of the sodium of a fast-food breakfast sandwich.

recipes.title: Maple Olive Oil Granola
recipes.blurb: Clusters that actually cluster: the trick is pressing it flat and not stirring it once it is in the oven. Forty minutes for two weeks of breakfasts.
steps: Heat the oven to 325°F. Toss everything except the dried cranberries together until every oat is coated.
Tip it onto a parchment-lined sheet pan and press it down hard and flat with a spatula. That compression is what makes clusters.
Bake 35-40 minutes, rotating the pan once but never stirring. Stirring is what gives you loose granola instead of clusters.
It will still be soft when it comes out. Let it cool completely on the pan, untouched, for at least 45 minutes — it crisps as it cools.
Break it into chunks and fold in the dried cranberries. Add dried fruit after baking; in the oven it turns to charcoal.
recipes.kidTweak: Bag some of the clusters on their own as a snack. It disappears faster than the cereal box does.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Olive oil instead of a neutral oil. It sounds odd and it makes granola taste like it came from a good bakery.
recipes.leftovers: Two weeks in a sealed jar; a month in the freezer.
recipes.heartNote: Oats, nuts, seeds, flax and olive oil, sweetened with a half cup of maple across twelve servings — around 5 g fiber and 7 g protein a portion, and a fraction of the sugar in most boxed granola.

recipes.title: Turmeric Tofu Scramble
recipes.blurb: Crumbled firm tofu with turmeric for color and a pinch of black salt for the eggy note. Ten minutes, high protein, no eggs at all.
steps: Press the tofu 10 minutes and crumble it by hand into uneven pieces — uniform cubes read as tofu, ragged crumbles read as scramble.
Cook the onion and pepper in the oil over medium-high for 5 minutes.
Add the tofu and cook 5 minutes without stirring much, letting some of it brown against the pan.
Add the turmeric, garlic powder, nutritional yeast, salt and pepper. The nutritional yeast is what makes it savory rather than beany.
Fold in the spinach until wilted. Serve on toast with avocado. A pinch of kala namak (black salt) at the end gives a genuinely eggy sulfur note if you can find it.
recipes.kidTweak: Serve it in a warm tortilla with cheese and salsa and it becomes a breakfast taco.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Let it sit still in the pan long enough to brown in patches. Constant stirring gives you a wet yellow pile.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 4 days and is excellent in burritos and fried rice.
recipes.heartNote: About 16 g of complete plant protein a serving with no cholesterol at all — the practical swap for someone told to cut back on eggs.

recipes.title: Overnight Slow Cooker Steel-Cut Oats
recipes.blurb: Five minutes before bed, breakfast for a week waiting in the morning. Steel-cut oats hold their chew where rolled oats turn to glue.
steps: Rub the crock with the teaspoon of oil — oats are the worst thing there is to scrub off a slow cooker.
Add the oats, soy milk, 3 cups water, apple, cinnamon and salt. Stir once.
Cook on low 7-8 hours. Set it before bed and it is done when you get up.
Stir in the maple, flax and half the walnuts in the morning. It will look too thick; a splash of milk brings it back.
Serve with the rest of the walnuts and the dried cranberries. Portion the leftovers into jars while it is still warm — it sets solid once cold.
recipes.kidTweak: Set out bowls of toppings — berries, banana, chocolate chips, nuts — and let everyone build. Same pot, six different breakfasts.
recipes.restaurantTouch: Salt in the oats. Unsalted porridge tastes like wallpaper paste no matter how much syrup goes on it.
recipes.leftovers: Keeps 5 days portioned in jars. Reheat with a splash of milk.
recipes.heartNote: Steel-cut oats plus flax plus walnuts: beta-glucan for LDL cholesterol, plant omega-3 from both the flax and the walnuts, and about 9 g of fiber a bowl.
